Jasleen, you asked how I got through losing the student council election. I'm Ritu, and honestly, I didn't do it by being brave.
For three days I did nothing. I skipped the canteen. I watched old cartoons. I let myself feel awful, and I told my roommate that was what I was doing, so she wouldn't worry.
On day four, I took a notebook and made two columns. In my control: my speech, my campaigning, how many classes I visited. Not in my control: the other candidate's popularity, the fact that the first years didn't know me yet.
Then one small thing. Not "I'll win next year." Just: I'll volunteer for the library committee this term. It took one email.
That was October. By February, people knew my name. Small things, one at a time. That felt more real than any big promise I made to myself.

qa.a: The library committee.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel during the first three days?
qa.a: Ritu felt awful and let the bad feeling be there, resting without forcing any plan.

qa.a: Splitting what was and wasn't in Ritu's control, then taking one small action, because a small win felt more real than a big promise.

qa.a: The roommate was probably less worried than she might have been, because Ritu had explained what was going on.

I share a flat with Damini, so I watched the week after the dance school audition from close up.
The result came on Monday: not selected. That day she barely left her room. I left food outside her door. She ate some of it. I didn't push.
On Wednesday, she came to the kitchen and made tea for both of us. She had a sheet of paper. Two columns. I read upside down: "My control: practice hours, the song I chose, my nerves." "Not my control: judges' taste, forty other dancers."
On Thursday, she didn't make any big announcements. She just asked me to film her doing one short routine on the terrace, one minute long, the part she'd messed up in the audition.
On Saturday, she sent it to her old teacher for feedback. I don't know exactly what she was thinking. But she hummed while doing the dishes.
— Zeenat

Sunday. Manoj missed the state sprint team by a tenth of a second. He went home, lay on the floor of his room and stared at the ceiling fan for hours. His coach, Aparna ma'am, messaged: "Rest this week. Don't train. Don't decide anything."
Wednesday. He felt a little less heavy. He sat with a notebook. In his control: starts, sleep, the two weeks he'd skipped stretching. Not in his control: the wind, the boy in lane four who'd had the race of his life.
The following Monday. He went to the ground at six. Aparna ma'am didn't mention the trial. She said, "Ten starts. Just starts." He did ten. On the eighth, his reaction was the fastest he'd ever done.
He wrote it down: "8th start, best ever." A small thing. He looked at it that night before sleeping, and for the first time in a week, he felt like a runner again.

qa.q: By how much did Manoj miss the state sprint team?
qa.a: By a tenth of a second.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel on Sunday?
qa.a: Manoj felt crushed and empty, lying on the floor staring at the fan for hours.

qa.q: How did Aparna ma'am's approach help Manoj recover?
qa.a: She told him to rest first and decide nothing, then gave him one small task, ten starts, so he could build on a real small win.

qa.q: What would change if Manoj had made big resolutions on Sunday?
qa.a: He might have pushed himself while still hurting, instead of resting and finding one clear thing to work on.

grounding: Illustrates a young athlete who rests after a failure, separates what was in his control, then takes one small step that becomes a small win.

I carried the rest home on the bus and didn't touch the oven for three days. My mother let me be. She just kept putting tea next to me.
